utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, good morning everyone. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Prosecutor, I would like to greet all the people present in the courtroom, the representatives of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, as well as all the people present in the courtroom. I shall now give the floor to Douglas Stringer, who would like to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel. I have one very brief matter to raise with the Court. I think out of caution it would be best to very quickly go into private session, and I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. The hearing has resumed, and I give the floor to Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Finlayson.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Finlayson, yesterday we left going through a series of UNMO reports relating to the targeting of the UNMO office in East Mostar, and the last report that we looked at was a document dated the 1st of December, 1993, and there it was reported that -- that the HVO committed to double its efforts to trap those shooting at the UNMO accommodation and vehicles. Now, I would like to continue today to show you some more reports relating to this issue in chronological order starting as of the 1st of December, and what I will do again is I will ask you to confirm for some of the reports I will just ask you confirm what has been reported and for others I may ask you some additional questions. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If we can then move first to Exhibit 07070, and this is an UNMO report dated the 7th -- the 7th of December. And if I could just draw your attention to page number 3 of this report, and I'll just ask you confirm, is it correct that under number 3 it's reported: "Sniping fire during the night on the accommodation of East Mostar team. Six impacts on the house."

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I then ask you to move to Exhibit 07255. My apologies. No, let's move to Exhibit 7177, and that's a report dated the 14th of December, a week later. Again, on page number 3, under 3: "Sniping activity continues around the UNMO location in East Mostar." Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We then move to Exhibit 7255. This is a report dated the 19th of December. And if I can direct your attention to page number 2. Under number 3, "Sniping activities on and around UNMO ECMM in East Mostar -- UNMO accommodation in East Mostar continues"?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Underneath that it reads, "23 wounded children accompanied by 22 relatives were transported out of East Mostar today during the operation angel." Do you recall anything about this operation angel?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall it, and I recall that we had some difficulty originally getting into East Mostar with that -- that convoy, but from -- from memory also it was a convoy that came up in the last minute, and I don't believe it was part of the UNHCR convoys. It was a -- from memory, it was a privately organised campaign by -- I think it was actually a British woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were civilians from East Mostar often evacuated from East Mostar. Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rarely actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I now ask you to move to Exhibit 7318, please. Now -- we're now moving close to Christmas. This is the 23rd of December, 1993, and if I can draw your attention to page number 2 of this report, and under number 5 it reads as follows: "Meeting SMO HVO revealed that SMO's plan to monitor the Christmas cease-fire would not be authorised." Can you elaborate a little bit on what's been reported here? What kind of cease-fire plan had you been discussing here with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There -- there had been a higher level cease-fire arranged at that time. Typically these cease-fires were signed in New York or Sarajevo or wherever, and very little direction was given on the coal face, so to speak. I essentially decided that I'd try and get that cease-fire to work in Mostar, and the general plan was to put an influx of UNMO and UNPROFOR people into Mostar at key points on both sides and eventually flood -- flood Mostar with -- with a presence to ensure that every small firing or, yeah, any firing could be located and dealt with in a more accurate manner than we were generally able to do. This involved a considerable amount of discussion between the local commander of the HVO, and I believe I spoke to both Lasic and Maric regards that. And I spoke to the armija about it. I think it's fair to say there was a reasonable amount of mistrust or a lack of confidence by the HVO on some aspects of the plan in that it relied on people putting theirselves on the line and actually staying there with the likes of the local battalion, which was SpaBat. I had a reasonable amount of support from the UNPROFOR, and I think they in fact posted about another 20 or 30 UNMOs into the area. After, I think, probably two to three days of going side by side East Mostar to West Mostar, I thought we were getting somewhere. The final decision ended up in General Roso's court, and in fact he gave the final no decision to that to go along with my plan late -- late the evening of around -- probably around the 21st or 22nd of December, which was a bit disappointing, but nevertheless ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If I could just ask you something about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my apologies to you and to my learned friend. Perhaps it's my folder containing these documents is not the neatest; however, Exhibit P 371A does not bear the date of the 23rd of December 1993 nor does item 2 under paragraph 5 address what is referred to in this question. Therefore I would require clarification. Are we talking about the same exhibits or have we perhaps got the numbers mixed up? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's my fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I don't know if there is confusion here on the number. I was referring to Exhibit 07318 and not 371A as has been here describe here in the transcript. 07318 and on the top of the page it clearly gives the date, 23rd of December, 1993. Well, 22nd of December, although above that it says UTC time 23rd of December. So it's -- it's around that time, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Considering the correction and the date being the 22nd of December, I think we can consider the matter clarified. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can see on the face of this document it was addressed on the 24th of -- 23rd of December, 21.44, and was received on the 23rd of December at 1.12. That's, at any rate, what's mentioned on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that is -- that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I was about to ask you just about this plan. Did this plan cover the town of Mostar or did -- was -- was the area more bigger than just -- can you -- can you say something about the area in which -- which this --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It focused on Mostar, and -- yeah. It -- it focused on just trying to get something happening in Mostar that maybe would escalate out if it was successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I now ask you to look at Exhibit 7368.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, I'm sorry. I have to put a question to the witness. I'm sorry for interrupting. Because if I wait for the examination-in-chief, we will have difficulty getting back to this question. Sir, the Prosecutor -- Prosecutor has showed you a whole series of documents stating, according to the Prosecutor, that the house where you were located was being targeted by the snipers. According to the theory of the Prosecutor, from what we understood it was the HVO that was firing. On looking at this document, which is dated at 22nd of December at 21.44, please turn to point OG, point 3. This paragraph says: "Attacks on UN personnel, equipment establishments once again," and so on and so forth. I see here that those that are firing are the Serbs. You identify them as such in this paragraph. In that case, how do you make a distinction between the HVO on the Serbs? Could you tell us this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, you're speaking about G -- G, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, that's under sector Sarajevo, sir. This is -- this is a BH command report and -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So this is in sector Sarajevo. Therefore, you have lifted any doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you to look at Exhibit 7368, and this is an UNMO report dated the 28th of December, 1993. And if I can direct your attention to page number 2 under F, 7, it reads: "Acute shortage of food items has been reported in East Mostar. Humanitarian aid reaching East Mostar has stopped since 18 December 1993." To what extent was the UNMO involved in -- in getting humanitarian aid to the population?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's fair to say that the majority of the time the UNMOs were aware of the -- of convoys going into the area. Often it was controlled by SpanBat because the convoys were typically accompanied by Spanish Battalion vehicles. It would normally have a -- an UNMO accompanying them and would -- who would really only get involved should there be problems at any check-point or -- or whatever. That was the typical case. It normally only -- sorry, not -- yeah. That was the typical case. Sometimes, I guess with any large system, we became aware of these convoys once they had experienced a problem, but typically our main role was negotiating -- helping negotiate their -- their arrival, but more -- more particularly we tended to get involved when they actually came across problems on the actual day of execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did problems often arise?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they -- they did, as they did throughout the former Yugoslavia, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was it easy to -- for humanitarian organisations to enter humanitarian convoys into East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, and from memory, to get access into the area was long and involved and often delayed - would be probably the accurate word - by the HVO. I think in most cases they would eventually get through, but it may be some time. And often, of course, the HVO who were in control of the entry to East Mostar would assume responsibility and state that it was it too dangerous for the convoys to proceed. But effectively they didn't -- they didn't get through, and we did have a period there where no food was getting in, and we had to rely on food drops from aeroplanes just simply to get food into the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We'll come to that -- back to that issue of air drops a little later. Let me just -- let's now continue and let me ask you to look at Exhibit 7489, and if I can direct your attention of this -- on this UNMO report to page number 6. And this is a report of the 6th of January, 1994, and I'll read out to you paragraphs (I) and (N) under 5. "In a meeting with HVO authorities they for the first time accepted the responsibility for the sniping of UNMO vehicle on 3 January 1994 and promised to resolve the incident once and for all -- once for all." Under (N): "The HVO acceptance of sniping UNMO vehicle is considered positive development which could eventually lead to the cessation of attacks on UNMO vehicles and accommodation." Let me just ask about this commander's assessment. Was this something that was your assessment? Did -- you drafted this or...

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- this report is a report from UNMO HQ Zagreb, which would have been, as I explained earlier, cut and pasted from the reports from my sector. That commander's assessment would have been done by me at the time, assuming I was there on the day at the time. If I wasn't there on the particular day, then I may not have -- my deputy may have put that comment down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did this -- this particular acceptance of responsibility by the HVO, did it improve the fact -- you know, did it improve the situation as it's hoped in this assessment?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I ask you then now to go to Exhibits 7633. And this is an UNMO report dated the 20th of January, 1994. And if I could ask you to look at page number 6, under 5(C): "Firing on UNMO accommodation in East Mostar is becoming a routine affair. Five times short arms rounds were fired around the accommodation. Two times short arms hit the accommodation." Can you confirm what's been reported here?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that was reported by my team at Mike X-ray 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I ask you then to move to Exhibit 7766. Now, this seems to be a consolidated report for a period of a week where all incidents of attacks and intimidation of UNMO personnel are being summarised in this report, and there's several references to Mostar, East Mostar, as well. But let me draw your direction to the 4th of February where it says: "BH South: At 1130A at Vrapcici 6 rounds were fired at the UNMO vehicle UNPF 3986. One 12.7 millimetre and one 7.62 millimetre hit the car." Can you comment on this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recall that incident. It involved from memory a fellow Kiwi UNMO as well as a British UNMO, I think, who were in the vehicle at the time, and they were essentially travelling south at the time on the main road north of Mostar when they received an incoming round, as reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And do you recall from where this incoming round came from and from --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially over -- straight over the Neretva River from the HVO-controlled area, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you -- could I ask you to look at the photograph which is Exhibit 10006, and maybe we can have that also put on the screen. Just wait for the photo to appear on the screen as well. Can you tell the Court what's being depicted on this photograph, witness?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially this is the -- the side of a -- an armoured vehicle or GMC vehicle that we had at the later stages in Mostar. The -- you can see the UN sign on the door there and the UN flag just -- you see the bottom edge of it. On the front driver's windscreen -- I've got to think about that. It may not be the driver's windscreen. Wrong side of the road. My apologies. The -- the large shell or damage there was -- it was the 12.6 [sic] indent. For information, these -- these vehicles are tremendously armoured, and the windscreen -- or, sorry, the side windows on those are probably around two inches thick. I guess due to the thickness the memory was the indentation was about half the thickness of the window. So that was the 12.7 round.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. And did this particular damage that we seen here on this car was that in fact the damage that was caused by the incident that was reported here on the 4th of February?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, we also see a little damage on -- on the window, you know, at the -- on the left side of the photograph. What can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was actually a separate incident which I think I mentioned yesterday when I myself was in the vehicle with Bo Pellnas, and that occurred -- that's only a small -- a small-arms fire, 7 mil, but that was received down the southern end of town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd just like to ask the witness to clarify what it means on the photograph when it says 10/94. Is it the 10th month of 1994 or what is it at the bottom, the numbers 10/94?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should mean that. What it is evidence of is a photographer that doesn't know how to set or turn that particular date item on. Unfortunately, I didn't take my instruction book to Bosnia, so it is confusing, but that does not mean it was taken then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When did you take that photograph? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall, it was the day after or even the -- no. No, I can't exactly, but it was shortly after, if not the day or the day after the incident. Actually, I'll take that back. I'm not -- not sure when I took that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to move to Exhibit 7875, please. And I draw your attention to page number 5 of this report. Again under paragraph 5. Under (C) it reads: "UNMO team Mostar east reports 21 small-arms rounds in the vicinity of their accommodation plus 12 small-arms hits of the accommodation itself." Then under (E): "SMO met with General Roso this afternoon. Topics were sniping of UNMO positions and possible solutions in the area. General Roso stated that everything would be solved in the Mostar area, would be solved within 10 days; even the targeting of UNMOs." Do you recall this meeting with General Roso in February 1993 [sic]?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, do I.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What can you tell us about this meeting?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at this particular meeting at that stage we had -- had actually set up an UNMO people in Posusje so we established very good communications with General Roso. The indication that things would be complete within 10 days, General Roso didn't really clarify, and consequently -- I mean, it turned out that more or less coincided with the cessation of -- of the war, but I wasn't aware of that at that time. The meeting went generally -- General Roso was genuine in -- in what he told us, and as he -- and -- and essentially indicated that he was making an effort to -- to make sure it occurred, but in hindsight he was obviously operating at a higher level than I was aware of at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I add a small question? Witness, did General Roso give any explanation as to why it would take 10 days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can -- I cannot recall that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we have a series of reports in a time line, and in each report mention is made of fire directed at the building where you had your office. Fortunately, apparently, nobody was killed or injured. This is a rather extraordinary situation. The UN people are targeted. Did this not call for action to be taken by you, more definite action, anti-sniping measures? Was this envisaged by your upper echelons? For instance, could the SpaBat have asked -- because they must have had snipers as well, could you have asked them for protection? This is only a guess. Could you have asked them to protect you, because it's rather easy to see where a sniper is and it's easy to shoot at him. Why were you so passive throughout this time mentioned in the reports? Do you have an explanation for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I tried to get support from other areas of Bosnia along those -- those lines. However, it never eventuated. I think there was. We accepted a certain amount of risk, and you can see by the reports that it was reported, and we did have discussion with Roso, General Roso on the matter as well as numerous discussions at the local level. We were really in the hands of BH command regards any greater our support that we got, but we certainly didn't get a lot of support from the local battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you said the local battalion. Which one, SpaBat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: SpaBat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] SpaBat. I see. And they failed to support you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be my assessment of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, I'd just like to correct something in the transcript. I think it could be vital. Page 13, line 15. It was wrongly recorded that the question related to February 1993. It should be February 1994. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Alaburic, for that clarification. Indeed, it should have been February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Finlayson, I have just one more document on this topic, and we now move to the 22nd of February, 1994, and that's the last report that I -- on this issue that I'd like to show you. 7 -- Exhibit 7930, page number 5. Page number 5 under 5(C). "Accommodation of East Mostar is still under sniper fire. Three times short arms rounds hit UN accommodation where nine rounds struck within 10 metres." Can you confirm what was written here?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that was reported by my team.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just a while ago you've been referring to air drops of humanitarian aid in East Mostar. Who -- who had organised these humanitarian aids, air drops? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were, as I recall, being organised via the UNMO -- UNMO headquarters in Zagreb. I think they were -- they were instigated by the UNHCR, representatives in -- in Mostar, and they were conducted by the Americans flying from Italy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you recall how many air drops of humanitarian aid --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't exactly. I think from memory there were probably only around two or three, I think. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And if I can ask you to look at the map that is behind you. Can you tell me where these drops of -- these air drops of humanitarian aid were dropped in the Mostar area?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, I can't. I had trouble thinking about this the other day, but they were essentially -- where are we -- in this area south -- in this area south of the town. We also had some up north near -- sorry, I've forgotten the name of it, Bjelebila [phoen] in this area up here or even further north, and we had another one in fact north into the Croatian pockets up north of Konjic and Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, were these air drops successful? Can you tell a bit more how these ...

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were successful. They were, I believe, successful in the north, north of Konjic. The first one we had in -- in -- south of Mostar was not successful in that it possibly didn't land in a good place and we lost, I think from memory, eight people through mines. We -- the one to the north, from memory, was successful. However, it was rumoured that the general population didn't get a lot of the aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can I just -- can I just --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: And.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: -- you said the first drop of this south of Mostar was not successful and you lost eight people?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say we lost eight people, people in the area that that team was responsible for, and that was the local population. I think they were reported as civilian, but I -- I can't confirm whether they were or not. And it was due to the fact that the -- the first air drop was done in the typical fashion where I think everyone can envisage that there was a large pallet of food dropped from a plane with a big parachute on it. So everyone tended to rush to these large packages. After -- after that debacle, it -- the Americans proposed dropping -- I can't remember what they were called, but like individual food packages, and these were dropped and some landed, from memory, and -- near the town, and the idea there was to stop the people rushing out to one big bundle, which happened in the south, and also to stop the -- or assist in ensuring that the general populous got the food that was dropped by spreading it out, small packages, spreading it out a bit more, and they were -- they were very successful, and I think the drops in fact continued probably for a bit longer up in Konjic, just thinking about it now. I think after we did a few -- a couple of drops in Mostar the convoys started to come through in that area. My memory is -- is a bit shaky on -- on times and numbers there but close.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look at Exhibit 6785, please. Now, this is a SpaBat report, and if I can ask you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe for this exhibit we would need to go into private session. This is an exhibit which is under seal, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If I can now direct your attention to Exhibit 6913, please. And page number 3. So this is the 26th of November, 1993. Under 3(F): "UNMOs continuing to monitor air drops hampered by deep snow. Some air drops continue to land in no man's land or other areas covered by HVO indirect fire." Now, do you recall that snow was a problem here as well?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, no, but the -- the dropping in no man's land was -- it was always going to be a problem because of the small area that they had, small target area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, moving to another topic now. Do you recall ever being tasked to investigate the presence of HV soldiers in the -- in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you recall what time this was?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would put the window of around between December 1993 and to the end of my time in BH South, which was -- well, yeah, early March.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look at Exhibit 7587. Now, this -- this is a report on the -- reporting on the -- on the HV presence in Bosnia. Do you recall this report, and do you recall what kind of investigations you did in order to find out whether HV soldiers were present in the region?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially we -- we tried to spread a net of patrols around the area, in particular in the areas where we had reported to us that it was likely that HV were operating. This was particularly in the area of Siroki Brijeg and also to the south of -- south of the sector -- we're getting close to the Croatian border there. It was considered that there were still Croatian army activity. Essentially the patrols that were sent out, and specifically some of them were -- specific patrols to go and look for the recorded over the weeks or the months that there was significant HV presence there at the time and it was building. We saw HV troops intermingled with HVO troops on check-points. There were also vehicles sighted around -- around the sector with -- with no licence plates and temporary HVO signs up on windscreens, et cetera. Then we also ran into the odd collection of -- or at least one collection of Croatian army soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I ask you also to look at Exhibit 7700. And if I can direct your attention to page number 2, part number 2. Is it correct that your name appears there on -- at the bottom of -- of the report?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, if you look at -- at paragraphs 2 and 3, I'll read it out, it says: "HV occupation of the area south of Stolac, Capljina, has been more blatant over the last weeks. Even the check-points along the road are sometimes manned with HV soldiers. They appear to always be in company with HV soldiers. There are a lot of trucks now operating without number plates now operating along the area. Over the next few days they have been noticed to be now displaying HVO plates in their windscreen." Number 3: "The insignia/badges have not -- had not been seen clearly at this stage but whilst some are simple HV with a simple chequered crest however it may repeat ... may bear some resemblance to that of the 5 professional brigade." Is it correct that you wrote these paragraphs I just read out?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I ask you about that last paragraph that I read out. You say at that there's a resemble -- a resemblance to five professional brigades. What are you referring here to?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I -- at this stage the five professional brigade was a known entity within the Croatian army, but my recollection of that and the specific details I'm afraid are no longer with me. I would say I had the, you know, a standard identification documentation that we used to identify people at the time, but I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, finally to -- to close off your testimony, is it correct that in February 1993 you were also again involved in -- in peace negotiations between the parties?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, in -- in relation to these peace negotiations, did you attend a meeting in February 1993 [sic] in which UNPROFOR General Cot and Mr. Jadranko Prlic participated as well?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look at --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, again I would like to draw everyone's attention to the year that was mentioned, and I would propose that my learned friend make appropriate adjustments.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Alaburic. I apologise. It should be February 1994 rather than 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look at Exhibit -- the last exhibit, 7771. And again, Your Honours, maybe for -- can we go into private session for this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Murphy, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honour, we have in addition to our time I understand been given some time by the Coric Defence. I'm not sure how much time we will use, but we -- we do have that time also. And I should note, Your Honour, that I think the Prlic Defence was originally due to start in the order of rotation, but due to I think a commitment, Mr. Karnavas's professional commitment, we have agreed to start and they will go at a later time during the rotation. Your Honour, as a preliminary matter, Mr. Bos has indicated to me something that I had not appreciated, which is that evidently the witness records his notes as having been given to the Prosecution confidentially and has indicated that it may be necessary to go into private session for references to the notes. In that case, we may be in and out of private session quite a bit, but I will have Mr. Bos confirm that for the record, if that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I just told Mr. Murphy before we started that -- at that Mr. Finlayson agreed that the notes could be handed over and disclosed to the Defence but under the conditions that it remain confidential to the public and that it would only be the Defence who would -- could use and look at those notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the first I hear of this. We had these notes for a long time, and I -- I don't see, you know, why this could not have been communicated early if that indeed was the case. Perhaps the gentleman didn't think that his notes would be used, but I don't think that this is the appropriate time to spring that on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, when we disclosed those notes we added a sentence saying that we -- we disclose those but under -- confidentially, and we actually underlined that sentence in -- in the disclosure letter of -- of the disclosure of these notes, so we did inform the Defence that they were disclosed confidentially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Finlayson.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: My name is Peter Murphy, and my colleague Ms. Nozica and I represent Mr. Bruno Stojic. We both have a number of questions for you. Let me indicate first that because you and I speak the same language, more or less, it will be necessary for us to remember to speak slowly and to leave a pause between question and answer for the interpreters. First of all, let me ask you about a witness statement that you made for the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you remember being interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor on the 31st of March and the 1st of April, 2003?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember being interviewed by Brent some of time ago. It would be around that time, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And after that interview, you did make a written witness statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You were given the opportunity to read that statement before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did -- was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And you signed it as being correct?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that this is the first time that you've testified in a case before the International Tribunal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And do I take it, then, that March 2003 was the first time that anyone from the Office of the Prosecutor asked you to recollect the events of 1993 to 1994?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But during the time that you were deployed in Bosnia and Herzegovina, you did make some personal notes?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And those notes, I take it, were made more or less at the time when the events were going on or shortly afterwards?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The events were -- the -- the notes were written up at the close of most days. That's why they're fairly brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you testified that before being deployed you had received some training in your duties as a UNMO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And you -- you told the Judges that that training was quite thorough.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The training in New Zealand was thorough. The training in Bosnia was -- sorry, in Zagreb was satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: When you gave your statement to the -- the Prosecutor, you made a statement about the training that you received in Zagreb. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need to refresh myself on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I can -- I can read it to you in the English version and you tell me if you -- if you remember this. It's from paragraph 9 of your statement in the English version. You said, and I quote: "I flew straight to Zagreb where I received another three days of training. This training was not very comprehensive and only included driving, first aid and a brief report on the situation in the former Yugoslavia. At no stage did I receive any training on international humanitarian law or anything to do with the laws or customs -- the laws and customs of war. I was not given any instructions on what to do if I witnessed anything that I thought was criminal or in breach of international treaties." Do you -- do you remember saying that to the -- in your statement?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have an issue with that statement. I would have said it, and I don't have an issue with it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And one other thing that I would like to read also from the following paragraph, paragraph 10, page 2 of the English version: "After the training, it is fair to say that we still didn't really know what our role was as UNMOs." Do you remember saying that in the statement that you gave?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember saying that. I -- it's possibly not well-worded and could be taken a little bit out of context or meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Well, now I want to ask you one or two things now about some things contained in your notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, perhaps for a brief time we may now go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: If we can just look at one more photograph there, Mr. Finlayson, of the house, which is 10001. I think it's the next photograph in the sequence. Which -- do you see that on the screen?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I think it's still -- we're still on ... You see that photograph, Mr. Finlayson, on the screen?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Which direction are we looking there? Which direction is the camera facing in that picture?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be just slightly higher than the arrow I indicated there. As I say, that's Spanski Square or in the direction of the Tito Bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So are we facing as from the house --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: West.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: West.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Again I just want to put this one more time and then I'll move on to my final question. Isn't it clear from these photographs that, as you said, that this is -- this house was in fact in the middle of the action?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't forget this was taken with a telephoto and -- and I can't remember the range, but quite a substantial one. So we were probably a kilometre from what I would term the action area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And yet in due course the decision was taken to relocate your team because it was considered for them to be -- it was considered too dangerous for them to be in the area.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that was regarding attacks on the staff that were not related to the accommodation at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And that was a decision with which you disagree.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Totally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. One further thing. If we could go back, please, to an exhibit that you were asked about yesterday, which is P 02293. Do you still have the Prosecution exhibits that Mr. Bos asked you about yesterday, Mr. Finlayson?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but it's coming up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: It's coming up on the screen. This is, as you may recall, a report that deals with your observation of prisoners, those who were being held at the Helo factory. Do you recall this document?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Mr. Bos asked you about certain parts of it, but no doubt because of lack of time omitted one or two things that I'd like to ask you to look at. If we can go to paragraph 3 of this document, please. If we could bring that up and magnify it a little bit. You see that paragraph three there beginning, "Persons in the prison were separated"?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You say there in the second sentence: "These people were anxious but insisted that they had been well treated by the HVO soldiers." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And then about halfway down that same paragraph is and sentence: "The men also were content with their treatment, with the exception that their diet had not included an army ration pack." And then finally if we could go to the next page, to paragraph 8 of the same document. You record there that, "all people requiring hospitalisation have been transferred accordingly. Numbers unknown." Is that right? That is what was written in the report.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I wrote. That would be -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Mr. Finlayson, that's all I have. My colleague Ms. Nozica has one or two questions for you. I want to thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: If Your Honour would allow us a moment to readjust. We won't take too much time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I see that Judge Antonetti is looking at the clock, but I'll try to use the remaining 10 minutes before the break to the best possible effect. My learned friend said that we could have the Coric Defence time to cross-examine, which I thank them for. Sir, I would like to pick up where my colleague left off asking you questions about the prisoners at Heliodrom. When you saw the Croat prisoners or in eastern Mostar, you wrote down in your diary that the conditions were poor but at least they were safe. The people you saw in the cellar. There was a basement room, 4 by 4 metres. You said something about that. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the prisoners in Mostar. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What about the prisoners at Heliodrom? You described their conditions too. Can we say that they, too, were certainly safe and were not at risk as far as the combat operations were concerned? They were outside the areas affected by combat operations. Could we say that, sir?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe you could say they were out of risk, but they were out of combat's way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I wanted to hear. I would like us now briefly to go back to that meeting that occurred on the 18th of April, which was discussed during this trial a great deal. I would like to ask you, sir, to go back to what you first said. Is it true that at the meeting you were assigned certain tasks until relation to the setting up of a centre for joint operations? Would I be right in saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I think we're at a different meeting here, but -- sorry, it was the -- what was the date? The --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The 18th of April. Yes, I'm going back to that meeting, the one that took place on the 18th of April. There's no need for you to go back to any of the documents. I'll tell you exactly when I need you to refer back to the documents. I'm just trying to take you back to the 18th of April and what happened at that time.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Sorry, I was looking at the 18th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, do you know that at the meeting it was agreed that both sides, I'm talking about the 18th of April, and I'm not trying to remind you of your diary, therefore, there's no need for you to be looking at your diary. It was agreed that both sides in Mostar should withdraw their soldiers back to barracks. Do you remember that sort of agreement being reached at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do -- do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know that both sides, commanders on both sides, as it were it, who had reached that agreement gave out appropriate orders for this job to be done? Is this something you're aware of, sir?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Before the break, I would like to briefly show you those two orders just to jog our memories. Before the break, I'm talking about my binder, this is EDS, this is 2D 00289. That is the binder that I'm referring to, 2D 00289. Can you please track that exhibit down, and then I'd like to ask you to tell me something. Have you got that, is sir?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Right. I see you're reading it already. I think we can agree that this is an order issued by the BH army, the 4th Corps, dated the 21st of April, 1993, signed by Mr. Arif Pasalic. Is that not a fact, sir? Referring to item 1, we see that this is an order about the withdrawal of soldiers to the Mostar barracks. That's what item 1 says. It says the 41st Motorised Brigade from 1300 hours will begin to withdraw all their units. And just for the sake of the transcript, this portion is illegible. I think the logical thing would be for this to be a reference to a materiel and technical equipment. The translation reads "MUP," the Ministry of the Interior. We'll try and see what it actually says and see if any amendments need making. And station them at the barracks of Konak and the South Camp. Do you remember this sort of agreement being reached that this was indeed what was agreed and that the BH army promised to withdraw their units to these locations specified in this order or, rather, the barracks mentioned?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: At 4, this is the order which Mr. Arif Pasalic, and he says that a mixed patrol of BH army and HVO military police will be set up to monitor the movement of soldiers within the city. It will seize weapons and long barrels from all -- from all soldiers of the BH army and the HVO carrying such weapons away from the front line. Can we please go to number 6. We see that a commission was set up comprising four persons, Mehic Redzo on behalf of the BH army, Mehic Redzo on behalf of the BH army, Adis Hondzo, likewise on behalf of the BH army, Mario Mikulic and Mato Knezovic on behalf of the HVO. This commission was to monitor the implementation of these assignments. And one thing I would like you to look at is number 10, that being the last thing that we do before the break. Number 10 reads: "Bridges within the city shall be taken over by UNPROFOR until a final resolution is found for the situation in the town by the civilian authorities." Can you agree with me that this very order in its entirety underlines precisely what was agreed at meetings at which you, too, received certain assignments, specifically in reference to soldiers being withdrawn to the Mostar barracks in order to allay such tensions as existed at the time?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report or this letter does -- I can't recall the actual letter, but it certainly does cover the points that I believe were -- were reached by -- by the parties at the meetings we attended.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'd like to move on to another area and another question, so I think this would be an opportune time to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have a 20-minute break and return at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've already had an hour and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. With the Coric Defence time, I still have 45 minutes, and Mr. Karnavas, or, rather, the Defence of Mr. Prlic has given me 15 minutes, so that makes it an hour more for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I think we can continue, sir. The last document that we saw was document 2D 00289. You don't have to look for it. I'm just going to ask you a few questions about the document and the facts linked to the document. Do you know where at that point in time, when Mr. Arif Pasalic issued this order, and he was the commander of the 4th Corps, do you know where in Mostar the command and headquarters of the 4th Corps was located?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I'd -- I'd actually have trouble to actually pinpoint that on the map now. It's -- it was on the western side over -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can I help you -- or, rather, would it help you if I told you it was in the Vranica building on the west side? Do you remember that? Do you remember that building where the headquarters of the 4th Corps was, that it was called the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- it -- it rings a bell, and I've sort of got a picture of it in my mind, but, I -- yeah, I'm really struggling with the location on the map-type thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you happen to know that the command of the 41st Motorised Brigade, that is to say the brigade that is mentioned in the order whose duty it was to dislocate to the Konak barracks, and South Camp was also located in that same building, that is to say in that same location where the command of the 4th Corps was? Do you remember that? Other witnesses testified about that, so if you remember, just say yes or no. It's not that important. We've heard from other witnesses, but I just wanted to see whether you knew about it.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll say no then.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In point 8 of this order it says that for the execution of this order the commander of the 41st Motorised Brigade will be responsible, the famous brigade, and the commanders of the subordinate units. Do you remember you had any contact at all with the commander of the 41st Motorised Brigade and whether you remember that it was the name that I'm going to tell you? Midhad Hujdur is his name. Does that sound familiar?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. At that point, I believe, the discussions with these parties were being handled particularly by General Bo Pellnas at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Now, since in point 10 it states that the bridges in town will be taken over by UNPROFOR, do you remember in that connection that at that point in time there were two bridges that were under the control of the BH army? The Tito Bridge was one, which it was also referred to as Musala Bridge, and the Old Bridge. One of those bridges was very close to your own base, so I assume that you know about that.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of both bridges, and I am aware of the requirement for UNPROFOR to be present at those bridges at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We'll come back to that, the question of bridges, in due course. I'd now like to show you another order issued by the HVO in conformity with the agreement, and it is document P 2030, and it is the last document in my own binder. It has a green sticker because it was put in last. Tell me when you've found it, please.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Now, this is a document which was issued by Brigadier Miljenko Lasic on the 22nd of April, 1993, and it also talks about the same matter, that is to say to put the HVO soldiers in the Tihomir Misic barracks, and the 3rd Brigade to be put up at Heliodrom. I'd just like us to look at point 4 together of the order. The orders are almost identical, but here Mr. Lasic confirms that a mixed team should be established combining the HVO and BH army and Mr. Mato -- Mate Knezovic will be delegated to the 1st, and Mr. Mario Mikulic to the HVO OZ JIH and it says the team will start operating immediately. Now, this order confirms what you said that both sides took the agreement seriously and took steps to implement the agreement at least judging by the orders they issued. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I -- that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, do you happen to know -- do you have any direct knowledge, indirect knowledge through the observers in town or whatever, whether the 41st Motorised Brigade of the BH army did in fact act pursuant to the around of Mr. Arif Pasalic and the agreement reached, and whether it did indeed put its units up in the Konak and South Camp barracks?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I will emphasise it's indirect because I was sent back in to the Spanish Battalion for-- on an errand for General Pellnas; however, my understanding is that, no, they didn't carry out those orders, and I believe General Pellnas actually got involved to try and prompt the -- the evacuation of the building, as required by the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I assume that you are referring to Hotel Mostar, which is where a unit was put up of the 41st Motorised Brigade, whereas I was referring for the record to the document that you were shown, which is Prosecution document P 02054, page 6 of that document. You don't have to look for it, but I'm just saying that for the record. Is that what you're referring to, that intervention by Mr. Pellnas when he took part in resolving this problem?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, you've prompted my memory on that one but, yes, that does -- that was the case, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know -- well, when you say that I prompted your memory, that the unit really did go to the barracks at Konak and South Camp, and do you have any information about what happened to the unit that was moved from the Mostar Hotel? What happened to it later on, I mean.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seem to recall that later they did get to the south barracks, but I think it's better for me to say maybe -- I think my -- my memory would be very inaccurate in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Your memory isn't too accurate. But for the record I'd like to indicate something that Witness CV stated on the 18th of January, 2007. The transcript page is 12599 to 12602, and it was the testimony of Witness -- of a witness who was in the Mostar Hotel, and he said that on that critical day after the intervention that they were moved from the Mostar Hotel, that the soldiers put on civilian clothing and went to the front line and not to the barracks, as was stated in the order. I just say that for the record, but you say you have no knowledge about that so I won't pursue the matter. But so that we can follow how these orders were executed or not, let us look at 2D 00406, the next document in the binder. Tell me when you've found it.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a report by the mixed commission of the BH army and the HVO, and it came into being on the basis of orders of the 21st of April and the 22nd of April. This report was signed, as we can see here, by two individuals. One an HVO representative, and his name was Mate Knezovic, and a representative of the BH army, Redzo Mehic. So the report is dated the 3rd of May, which means some 10 days after the commission was established. And I'd like us to look at the second sentence where it says: "The mixed police patrol inspected all the facilities which should have been emptied, but the situation is the same as it was a week ago, which mainly refers to the left bank. As the mixed patrol was inspecting the bridge, the commander of the 1st Mostar Brigade told them that they had no business inspecting there. We ask that the commission, the joint commission that is, with representatives of both parts, we ask that the OZ command level for the South-eastern Herzegovina solve this with the corps command. "The commission demands another urgent meeting to be held for further instructions because the work of the commission has been obstructed because the joint order was not implemented, or due to the failure to implement a joint order." I know you haven't seen that, but can we agree that was roughly how you remember the events, and that quite obviously from this joint report it would emerge that the BH army, and we here see mention of the left bank that it did not act upon the order to relocate the units and send them back to barracks. Would that be the proper interpretation of this report?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You will remember from an earlier order by Mr. Arif Pasalic, and you said you remembered that one, that the bridges were supposed to be placed under the control of UNPROFOR. Now from, this report does it emerge that quite obviously that was not done, because it says here that the commission did tour the bridges but that the command of the 1st Motorised Brigade told them that they had nothing to control there, and so the logical conclusion would be that UNPROFOR did not assume control of the bridge, but that at that time, at least, it was still the 1st Motorised Brigade of the BH army which had control of the bridge?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sequence of events I'm unsure of, but certainly UNPROFOR took up position at the -- at the bridges at some point. The date I wouldn't be able to give and whether it was before or after this particular point. However, I do appreciate that they did not maintain that -- that -- their position at the bridges.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I agree with you when it comes to the bridges. And let's look at the last set of -- the last document in the set. It is 2D 00452.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Fine. Let's take a look at the date. It is the 29th of April, 1993, and you can see what it says here. It is an order by Mr. Hujdur, and I asked you a moment ago whether you remember that he was the commander of the 41st Motorised Brigade. You weren't able to remember that, but we see his name here. So let's see what the order says. It says: "Upon receipt of this order immediately ban all motor vehicles from crossing the Musala bridge." Can you and I agree that the Musala bridge was in fact the Tito Bridge? Do we agree there?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually can't recall it being called the Musala bridge, but we always referred to it as Tito's bridge, but it appears that that's what they're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But please believe me when I tell you it's another name for the bridge. Let's see what point 2 says: "Only vehicles which have permits to use the Musala Bridge issued by the command of the 41st Motorised Brigade can be allowed to cross it." So the conclusion on the basis of this would be that the 41st Motorised Brigade had control of the bridge and that it wasn't UNPROFOR who controlled the bridge. Am I right in saying that? You said that you know that at one point UNPROFOR did have control, but you thought that it was for a brief period, and is this borne out by this document?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of this, this document, and I cannot recall which -- sorry, I cannot recall whether the bridge was in fact controlled by the 41st Motorised Brigade. However, this letter would indicate that -- as you asked, that they did have control of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But you have no knowledge that's what things were like at the end of April, or do you have knowledge that it was that way? You were close by. Do you know that vehicles could only pass if they had a permit from the command of the 41st Motorised Brigade? Do you know about that? Yes? No? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall there being antagonisation. The exact details of it, this -- this -- I -- I can recall it, but not in detail, I guess is what I'm saying. I can't recall exactly whether it was a permit and whether it was from the 41st Battalion. It was from the Muslim side, sorry about that, but the -- the details of the letter, I'm sorry, 13 years have gone by.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. But we can conclude in what you said that if the Spanish Battalion took control of the bridges in conformity with this order that it lasted for a very brief period.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, sir, with respect to the documents we've seen, and I wanted to show you documents which indicate the problem, highlight the problem of the relocation of the BH army and their moving out of the Mostar area, the area of the whole town. Now, do you know that during that period of time most of the conflicts that took place were conflicts between the HVO and the BH army, precisely because the BH army did not implement a single agreement reached, not even its own orders and agreements, and moved its units during that period of time, and they did not go back to barracks, as had been agreed? Do you know that that was one of the main bones of contention between the HVO and the BH army?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm obviously not aware of what goes on in the headquarters of HVO and what decided on their reasons to conduct an attack. I do agree, however, that there was a certain -- a good amount of antagonism regards this refusal to -- to move over to the southern and Konak barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have to note for the interpretation that you must be a witness they like very much, because you speak very slowly and of course everything can be translated and be recorded. However, I don't know whether we'll be able to get through everything I wanted to get through at that pace, but let's move on. And of course I think it is more important to have an exact transcript and record of what is being said, and we'll be able to get through other matters with other witnesses perhaps. But I'd like to take you back now to the 18th of April again. After the 18th of April you said that immediately after that, in a patrol you left and went towards the north to a place called Ostrozac, and we saw your diary today -- well, you've already answered some questions related to that, and you said that it was a control, a check-point by some Croats who were surrounded by the BH army. Now, I'd like to ask you to take a look at the following document. It is P 02107. It is a report, in fact, by UNPROFOR, and the date is the 21st of April. That's what it refers to. 1993. Could you just take a look at page 3 in the English version, and it's also on page 3 in the Croatian version. As I said, the report is -- is dated the 25th of April. Take a look at the way the events in Jablanica are described in this report, and then just tell me whether you remember or not, or whether you had any information and knowledge about these events, and whether they were in fact the events that in one way or another -- or, rather, events that you recorded, something in your diary about conduct towards civilians and how the two sides behaved towards civilians. Have you found page 3? It says, "Jablanica and Konjic," and it says, "the situation is extremely tense," and then on the 25th at 0730 hours in the area of responsibility the civilians and soldiers of the HVO are withdrawing. Some of them are wounded. And this took place at one and a half kilometres away from Ostrozac when they stopped a reconnaissance unit that was patrolling and required -- demanded protection. They even took refuge behind an APC stating that if they did not receive protection the armija would kill them. They also said there were many casualties from the last combats. And it says that among the people there were around 60 HVO soldiers and around 200 women, children, and elderly. And while the platoon was awaiting orders the BH army troops approached the locality and started shooting above the refugee's heads. The BH army leader told the platoon commander to leave within five minutes or else they would open fire. The BH soldiers had anti-tank weapons with them. The platoon commander stayed. And then it goes on to say that the civilians were in great danger and the BH army personnel disarmed the HVO soldiers. Some of the BH army left. Others stayed on, and the Spanish Battalion tried to protect them. An evacuation was agreed upon, and buses arrived but they weren't allowed to leave. And it says negotiations at all levels are taking place whereby preparations should be taken to see to the refugees if they stayed. Do you remember anything linked to this incident? It was a rather major incident with civilians involved, and all this happened the day after you left the area. But do you have any knowledge about this?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negative. I can't recall this incident purely because I would say it -- it appears to be a SpaBat report, and it doesn't appear to have come from the military observer organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That isn't what I was saying. It definitely wasn't produced by a military observer organisation. I'm asking you whether you have any knowledge of the incident itself, since this was more or less an area covered by the commissions set up on the 28th of April. They were supposed to look into what was going on, on the ground in that particular area, which includes this incident. They could possibly have reported to you and to the information centre that had been set up. Do you have any knowledge of what or not? If not, please, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's fine. Sir, something you said several times today. The OTP were asking you certain questions and my learned friend, Mr. Murphy, was asking you several questions about the Croat pocket, as you described them to the north of Konjic and Jablanica. Can we please look at a particular document together so that we may see whether this is the pocket you have in mind and whether you know anything about the destiny of all these people who stayed for a long time in these Croats pockets. This is 2D 00450. Before we embark on this, I would like to draw your attention to page 69. You probably have the transcript right in front of you. Pages 12, 13, and 14. I asked you if you had any knowledge of that. You said no. The transcript, however, says that the microphone was not activated. You agree with me, sir, that you said no, you didn't have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I seem to be running out of time on the one hand. On the other, I think you can be very helpful, considering your knowledge of certain situations. This document is dated the 23rd of April, the 23rd of April, 1993. So this is the time when these commissions were it particularly active, the commissions looking into the situation on the ground. I'm showing you this also because at one point in your testimony you said that the Croats to a high degree held it against you and other institutions that you didn't pay enough attention to what was going on with the Croats in the north of Bosnia and Central Bosnia and outside Bosna. This sometimes caused them to be less cooperative than they otherwise might have been. There was this document about the suffering of those people and the previous document an UNPROFOR report talking about those people who happened to be there as a result of military operations. We have an entire document about the suffering of certain villages that were burnt to the ground and Croats were expelled from them. I'm talking about the Konjic area. That's where the villages were. I'm about to ask you a question. I'm just trying to focus on something particular here. It says "B," the Konjic village area and the hamlets in the surroundings. The town of Konjic itself is under the control of Muslims, and Croats have been imprisoned or driven away to the village of Celebici. According to our information there are about 300 Croats in that camp. The Croats who were expelled from the town were put in the villages of Turija, Zabrdze, and Zaselje. We know nothing about their destiny. It goes on, the document goes on, but let me ask you this: First of all, do you know for a fact that this is something that happened in Konjic? There were military operations afoot there, and the town was seized by the Muslims, expelling the Croats in the process, and do you know there was a prison in Celebici where the Croats were being held at the time? Lastly, does this tell you anything: Turija, Zabrdzje, and Zaselje, could this be one of the Croat pockets you refer to, sir?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could be.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It could be -- is yes an answer to everything that that I've asked you --

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's take one step at a time, as my learned friend Mr. Karnavas is wont to say. You do know that these operations took place in the Konjic area and that the Croats were indeed expelled from the area. Is that the sort of information that you had at the time? I'm not asking you in relation to each of these villages, but general knowledge of this situation taking place in the area at the time.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly this -- this form of report of relocation of personnel were common, and, as you picked up, that was the purpose of the joint commission. And the -- certainly the Celebici area comes to mind, and Konjic was definitely under Muslim -- or came under Muslim control, and I also believe that Croats were relocated. However, the investigation of those areas were -- I wouldn't be able to report in detail on those specific small villages. I can't -- can't relate to those without referring to obvious reports. But this would be a typical document. It's not addressed to the -- to the commission, but that -- that sort of discussion would -- would then be -- typically in the joint commission, it would be broken down to it a priority agreed by parties, and we'd go -- that's where we got to the Ostrozac. That was the first priority, and so on and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm slightly concerned by the term you seem to be using, relocated. What does that mean? These are Croats from Kiseljak [as interpreted]; right? Your information seems to suggest that, too, they were imprisoned in Celebici. If we agree with this UNPROFOR report suggesting that they were desperate. They got as far as the road and crawled under UNPROFOR vehicles because they were scared of people taking revenge. Would we call these people relocated or perhaps driven out, expelled? Can we be using the same terms when speaking of HVO action and BH army action? I'm just asking this based on your information. Could we say that these people were relocated or were these Croats in fact expelled from the Konjic area, the BH army having taken control of the area? Would that be a more appropriate term to use, or is this simply something that your investigation never looked into?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself did not look into that. It was a -- it was an incident that involved the Spanish Battalion, and they -- they dealt with it. The use the term relocation is -- is appropriate for me, for both sides, when I don't know the facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I wish to thank my learned friend. Page 72, line 9, it should read Konjic, whereas the transcript reads Kiseljak. You confirmed, as far as I remember, your knowledge of the fact that in the village of Turija, Zabrdzje, and Zaselje, that those were the Croatian pockets that were at one point entirely surrounded by the BH army. You say that you do have knowledge of that, sir, don't you?

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not confirm that I had knowledge of those particular villages. As I said, I cannot recall the exact names of the villages up there, so I would be -- and without a situation map, I would not be able to comment. What I will say is that there were a -- I recall there were a number of villages that became very isolated with Croats in them in that area, and it became a very tricky region to actually even get in and patrol due to access reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were those in fact the same villages that were in the midst of a humanitarian crisis? You talk about humanitarian aid shipments to those villages stranded inside those Croat pockets and entirely surrounded by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: GRANT FINLAYSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, the names I'm not familiar with, but I with assume that they were the areas that we were trying to get aid into, yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm not trying to side-track you, on this is how I'll prove it: I will show you a report dated the 3rd of June, 1993. It's in an OTP binder.
